name: Authoritarianism
summary: Authoritarianism is rule by a single leader or small group holding ultimate, practically unlimited authority, with the state supreme over other organizations, political pluralism and participation limited, dissenters repressed and individual rights subordinate to the government's needs. Scholars after Linz distinguish it from totalitarianism by its lack of an elaborate guiding ideology, so it says little about economics, religion or social policy.
scope: The ideal type of authoritarian rule as defined in the reference scholarship (Linz's limited pluralism, limited mobilization and mentalities in place of an ideology, as set out in Encyclopedia.com, the Bielefeld InterAmerican Wiki and the ECPS Dictionary of Populism). It excludes totalitarianism, specific regime types (military, party, bureaucratic) taken as separate subjects, and the psychology of right-wing authoritarian followers, which the defining sources do not present as the doctrine itself. Economic, religious, social and foreign-policy statements are left null because the defining sources say regimes differ there.

sources.title: Authoritarianism (Encyclopedia.com, Gale reference entry)
sources.author: Encyclopedia.com
sources.usedFor: Defining features of authoritarianism: ultimate authority in one leader or small group, supremacy of the state over organizations, limits on mass participation, repression of dissent, rights subject to the needs of government, little ideology.

sources.title: Authoritarian Regimes (InterAmerican Wiki, Universität Bielefeld)
sources.author: Hans-Joachim Lauth
sources.usedFor: Linz's three marks (limited pluralism, limited participation, mentalities not ideology), what authoritarian regimes do not maintain, legitimation and repression.

sources.title: Authoritarianism (Dictionary of Populism, ECPS)
sources.author: European Centre for Populism Studies
sources.usedFor: Concentrated power kept by repression, Linz's four qualities, obedience to authority as the justification, regime tools.

missingStatements.text: Political opposition and independent organisations should be suppressed to preserve order.
missingStatements.rationale: Encyclopedia.com and ECPS describe repression of dissent and exclusion of potential challengers, with limited pluralism, as defining features.

missingStatements.text: Obedience to legitimate authority is a moral duty of citizens.
missingStatements.rationale: ECPS names as authoritarianism's prominent justification the view that unquestioning obedience to authority is crucial to social order.

missingStatements.text: Elections should be managed so that the incumbent ruler or ruling group does not lose power.
missingStatements.rationale: ECPS and Lauth describe managed, non-competitive or fraudulent elections that entrench authoritarian rule, though some regimes hold none.
missingStatements.declined: Weak (+1) and disputed among adherents; managed elections are covered loosely by suppress-opposition, one-party-rule and unlimited-reelection.

notes: Later pass under rules 7 (2026-11-13). The first pass leaned on Wikipedia, a Hobbes chapter and Altemeyer's psychological scale; none is tied to authoritarianism as a doctrine by the defining sources, and the old 0 answers rested on a general remark that regimes vary, so they are nulled. Searched for fuller sources: Altemeyer's The Authoritarians (only a table of contents was reachable), Brooker and Linz-Stepan excerpts on is.muni.cz (bot check; left alone), Britannica (blocked). Themes searched in the three reference entries: government, liberty, means, economy, society, world; economy, religion, culture, ecology, technology and globalism hold no stated position. Lines the validator names (nationalism, ethnonationalism, minority rights, patriarchy, national sovereignty) were searched in the same entries and in Lauth's note that regimes legitimate themselves by patriotism, nationalism, modernization or order; the sources present these as varying mentalities, not tenets, so they stay null.
